rule_sets.title: Western Australia: houses, extensions and granny flats
rule_sets.description: Development approval, building permits, BAL assessments and demolition permits in WA for houses, extensions and ancillary dwellings.
limitations: We don't know your zone, R-Code (density code) or your council's local planning policies, so we can only say whether you may need development approval.
Your council's local planning scheme and policies are not encoded. PlanWA shows your zone, R-Code, bushfire prone areas and heritage places.
Constraints like heritage, bushfire and flooding come from your answers. Not ticking one doesn't mean it doesn't apply.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a registered building surveyor or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: Development approval may be needed, depending on zone, R-Code and design

outcomes.title: You may need development approval from your council
outcomes.detail: In WA a single house, extension or granny flat that meets every deemed-to-comply standard in the Residential Design Codes (R-Codes) Volume 1 is usually exempt from development approval under clause 61 of the deemed provisions. You need approval if your design relies on a design principle instead (for example a smaller setback or more site cover), if the place is heritage-protected, or if your local planning scheme or a local development plan says so. Check your zone and R-Code on PlanWA, then ask your designer to check the plans against the deemed-to-comply standards.

approval.pathway: Development approval under your local planning scheme (Planning and Development Act 2005)

evidence.title: Site plan with setbacks, open space and existing buildings
Certificate of title from Landgate, with any easements and restrictive covenants

payload.task: Look up your zone and R-Code on PlanWA and check the design against the R-Codes deemed-to-comply standards

rules.notes: MAY_APPLY because we don't know the zone, R-Code or whether the design is fully deemed-to-comply.

outcomes.title: Heritage listing: you likely need development approval
outcomes.detail: The clause 61 exemption for houses that meet the R-Codes doesn't apply to a heritage-protected place: one on the State Register of Heritage Places, on your council's Heritage List or in a heritage area. Expect to need development approval, and a heritage impact statement for bigger changes. Work to a State Register place is referred to the Heritage Council. Check the listing on inHerit.

approval.pathway: Development approval under your local planning scheme (Planning and Development Act 2005)

evidence.title: Heritage impact statement, if council asks for one

payload.task: Check the place's heritage listing on inHerit and ask council about heritage requirements

rules.title: Bushfire prone areas need a BAL assessment

outcomes.title: Bushfire prone area: you likely need a BAL assessment
outcomes.detail: If your land is on the Map of Bush Fire Prone Areas, the Building Code's bushfire construction rules apply to houses, granny flats and attached structures. A Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) assessment by an accredited bushfire practitioner sets the construction standard and goes with your building permit application. Under State Planning Policy 3.7, a high BAL (BAL-40 or Flame Zone) can also mean you need development approval with a bushfire management plan.

approval.authority: An accredited bushfire planning practitioner, checked by your building surveyor
approval.pathway: BAL assessment to AS 3959 for the building permit; State Planning Policy 3.7 for planning

evidence.title: BAL assessment (or BAL contour plan) by an accredited practitioner

payload.task: Check the Map of Bush Fire Prone Areas and order a BAL assessment

outcomes.title: Flood-prone land: check floor levels with council
outcomes.detail: Councils can set minimum floor levels and other controls on flood-prone land through the local planning scheme or local planning policies. This can remove the exemption from development approval. Ask council what applies before you finalise the design.

payload.task: Ask council about flood controls and minimum floor levels for your lot

rules.title: Clearing native vegetation

outcomes.title: Protected vegetation: you may need a clearing permit
outcomes.detail: Clearing native vegetation in WA generally needs a clearing permit under the Environmental Protection Act 1986 unless an exemption applies, and councils can protect significant trees through their scheme. Check before you clear any part of the site.

payload.task: Check whether clearing on your site needs a native vegetation clearing permit

rules.notes: Clearing permits are administered by the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation; not verified this session.

outcomes.title: You will almost certainly need a building permit
outcomes.detail: Building a house, extension or granny flat in WA needs a building permit from your council (the permit authority). You can lodge a certified application (WA BA1 building permit application) with a certificate of design compliance from a registered private building surveyor, decided in 10 business days, or an uncertified application (WA BA2 uncertified building permit application) checked by the council, decided in 25 business days. Get development approval first if you need it.

approval.authority: Your local government as permit authority
approval.pathway: Building permit under the Building Act 2011 (certified or uncertified)

evidence.title: Energy efficiency assessment to the Building Code
WA BA3 certificate of design compliance (certified applications)

payload.task: Choose a certified or uncertified building permit application and line up a building surveyor

rules.title: Demolishing the existing house needs a demolition permit

outcomes.title: If you knock down the existing house, you need a demolition permit
outcomes.detail: Demolishing a house in WA needs a demolition permit from your council (WA BA5 demolition permit application). Asbestos must be removed by a licensed removalist, and services must be disconnected first. In a heritage-protected place, demolition also needs development approval.

approval.authority: Your local government as permit authority
approval.pathway: Demolition permit under the Building Act 2011

payload.task: If the existing house is coming down, apply for a demolition permit

rules.notes: MAY_APPLY because a new house on a lot with an existing house may keep it.

rules.title: Houses don't need an occupancy permit

outcomes.title: No occupancy permit for a house, but tell council when you finish
outcomes.detail: In WA, houses (Class 1a) and sheds or garages (Class 10) don't need an occupancy permit. When the work is done, the builder named on the permit must lodge a WA BA7 notice of completion with the council within 7 days.

rules.notes: The 7 day notice of completion period is from memory of the Building Act 2011; not re-read this session.

rules.title: Ancillary dwellings up to 70 m2 can be exempt

outcomes.title: Up to 70 m2: your granny flat may not need development approval
outcomes.detail: Since April 2024 an ancillary dwelling (granny flat) with an internal floor area of up to 70 m2 needs no development approval if it meets every deemed-to-comply requirement in R-Codes Volume 1. There's no minimum lot size, most don't need a parking bay, and anyone can live in it, including a tenant. It still needs a building permit, and heritage, bushfire or local scheme controls can still trigger development approval.

outcomes.title: Over 70 m2: you likely need development approval
outcomes.detail: A granny flat bigger than 70 m2 doesn't meet the R-Codes deemed-to-comply size limit, so it needs development approval assessed against the design principles, or it may be treated as a second house (grouped dwelling) if your R-Code allows that.

approval.pathway: Development approval under your local planning scheme (Planning and Development Act 2005)

payload.task: Ask council or a town planner whether a granny flat over 70 m2 can be approved on your lot

rules.title: An ancillary dwelling goes with a single house

outcomes.title: An ancillary dwelling sits with the main house
outcomes.detail: An ancillary dwelling is a self-contained dwelling on the same lot as a single house. It can't be sold separately unless the land is subdivided.

outcomes.title: No house on the land yet
outcomes.detail: An ancillary dwelling must be on the same lot as a single house. If you build it first, or at the same time as the main house, check with council how it will be assessed.

outcomes.title: You need subdivision approval from the WA Planning Commission
outcomes.detail: In WA, subdividing land into 2 or more freehold or survey-strata lots is approved by the Western Australian Planning Commission (WAPC), not your council. Your surveyor or town planner lodges WAPC Form 1A subdivision application through the WAPC's eLodgement system. The WAPC asks council and service agencies for advice and sets conditions. Your R-Code sets the minimum and average lot sizes.

approval.pathway: Subdivision approval under Part 10 of the Planning and Development Act 2005

evidence.title: Proposed plan of subdivision with lot sizes and existing buildings

payload.task: Ask a licensed surveyor to check your R-Code lot sizes and prepare a subdivision plan

outcomes.title: After approval: clear conditions, then Landgate issues new titles
outcomes.detail: Once the WAPC approves your subdivision, you meet the conditions (often Water Corporation and Western Power connections, crossovers and demolition), get clearances from the council and agencies, and your surveyor lodges the deposited plan with Landgate. The WAPC endorses the plan and Landgate issues a certificate of title for each lot.

payload.task: Plan the time and cost of clearing subdivision conditions before you sell or build

rules.title: Bushfire and subdivision

outcomes.title: Bushfire prone land: expect a BAL contour plan
outcomes.detail: Under State Planning Policy 3.7, a subdivision in a bushfire prone area must show that each lot can be built at BAL-29 or lower. The WAPC usually wants a BAL contour map and bushfire management plan from an accredited practitioner with the application.

approval.pathway: BAL contour map and bushfire management plan for subdivision

payload.task: Get a BAL contour map before you lodge the subdivision

rules.notes: BAL-29 lot threshold is from SPP 3.7 as previously published; not re-read this session.

rules.title: Change of use may need development approval

outcomes.title: You may need development approval for the new use
outcomes.detail: Whether a new use needs approval depends on the zoning table in your local planning scheme. Some uses are permitted, some need approval with or without advertising, and some aren't allowed in the zone. Clause 61 also exempts some changes of use, such as a change to a permitted use with no building work, depending on your scheme.

approval.pathway: Development approval under your local planning scheme (Planning and Development Act 2005)

evidence.title: Site and floor plans showing the new use and parking
Short report on hours, staff, customers and parking

rules.title: A change of building class needs a permit and occupancy permit

outcomes.title: You may need a building permit and an occupancy permit
outcomes.detail: If the new use changes the building's class under the Building Code (for example a house becoming a shop or office), you need an occupancy permit for the new classification (WA BA9 occupancy permit application), and a building permit for any work like fire separation, access or toilets.

approval.authority: Your local government as permit authority
approval.pathway: Occupancy permit under the Building Act 2011

Search your address to see the local planning scheme zone, the R-Code (density code, such as R20), bushfire prone areas and heritage places. outcomes.title: Your project may need development approval
outcomes.detail: Most development in WA needs development approval unless clause 61 of the deemed provisions or your local planning scheme exempts it. Larger projects, generally worth millions of dollars, can be decided by a development assessment panel instead of council. Talk to council's duty planner about your project.
